paper_title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances have extended large language models (LLMs) from single-turn chatbots to collaborative agents that complete long-horizon tasks in dynamic environments (Patil et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). Such agents must not only master scalable tool set, but also orchestrate diverse tools into executable long-horizon chains. Because tools are the atomic units of agent execution, how tools are organized and composed at scale has become foundational question for expanding agent capability (Anthropic, 2024; Li et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025). To scale tool use, recent work follows two main routes. One family, exemplified by Simia (Li et al., 2025) and GenEnv (Guo et al., 2025), treats the LLM as an implicit textual world model and generates simulated feedback from tool specifications and interaction histories. These methods are inexpensive, but their feedback is prone to hallucination and state consistency is difficult to guarantee. The second family explicitly reproduces interaction logic by synthesizing executable tools together with environment databases: it extracts or constructs an underlying database from real service theme, generates matching tools, and synthesizes tasks with verifiable outcomes (Dong et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Later systems further evolve whole interaction stacks or repair environments from execution feedback (Dong et al., 2026b; He et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026). Despite these advances, existing paradigms still follow Data-Centric Environment Synthesis: synthesize the underlying database and thematic scenario first, and only then derive tools and tasks. This ordering has three inherent limitations: Toolfunctionality mismatch. Executable tools are synthesized from the environment database and theme description, so their parameter logic easily diverges from real tool interface definitions. Agents consequently learn synthetic tool protocol rather than operations transferable to real tool ecosystem. Inauthentic tool orchestration. Existing work builds tool-link graphs and synthesizes tasks through random linking or shallow LLM judgments, so the resulting links lack authenticity. Real tool services are moreover unstable and noisy, and their logical relations are hard to establish subjectively. Lack of cross-environment task synthesis. Current task synthesis relies on the data and rules of single environment, whereas real-world tasks routinely span several environments. Because tools are locked inside their own sandboxes, cross-environment composition has no explicit reachability relation, and long-horizon complexity cannot grow naturally. Together, these limitations share single root cause: Data-Centric Environment Synthesis presumes realistically synthesized environment and derives tool composition from it, reversing the dependency that governs real agent execution. How to synthesize agent training data that preserves real tool orchestration across diverse environments therefore remains an open challenge. Our starting point is that, within agent execution, tools are the atomic units of capability growth, not static environment data. As illustrated in Figure 1(a)(b), Tool Space that has not yet been explicitly modeled always lies between an agent and its underlying environment databases, and the relations among tools naturally connect an extensible environment ecosystem. natural path is therefore to model the real connectivity and state transfer among tools, and to build crossenvironment tool-graph layer on top of these relations. The complexity of synthesized tasks then arises from expanding the real tool-composition space, rather than from the data scale of any single environment. Following this insight, we propose ToolSpace, tool-centric framework for cross-environment agent data synthesis. Unlike Data-Centric Environment Synthesis, ToolSpace does not mine new environment ecosystem from scratch; it follows Trace-to-ENV principle (Long et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2 2026): it first reconstructs scalable, explorable tool space from execution traces, then synthesizes long-horizon agent tasks across the tool and environment clusters connected in this space. ToolSpace consists of two stages: Tool Space Exploration. We extract tool calls from real-world execution traces and mine data, state, and retry links with deterministic rules, building scalable tool-composition graph. Tightly coupled tools are clustered into environment clusters; an underlying database is synthesized on demand only for operation environments, while original tool returns are reused directly otherwise. This preserves tool-composition relationships while substantially reducing environment synthesis cost. Cross-Environment Verifiable Task Synthesis. Over the ToolSpace graph, State-Aware Random Walks with Rollback Sampling sample state-compatible successors by edge weight and execute them step by step, retaining only chains that execute end to end under runtime-observed state transitions. Each retained walk is then decompiled into natural-language task with assertion-based verification scripts, yielding training samples that can be replayed and audited across environments. To validate ToolSpaces ability to flexibly synthesize complex cross-environment tasks, we anchor the full pipeline to AutomationBench (Shepard and Salimans, 2026) and 𝜏3-Bench Banking (Shi et al., 2026), two long-horizon agent benchmarks and extend their difficulty, producing AutomationBench Pro and 𝜏3-Bench Banking Pro. The upgraded versions exceed the standard ones in task difficulty and number of environments crossed. On AutomationBench Pro, seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points relative to the standard version (Figure 1). In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We identify limits of data-centric synthesis: reverse-synthesized tools mismatch real tool semantics, tool graphs lack execution evidence, and tasks are confined to single-environment complexity; and we then propose Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis. We propose ToolSpace, which reconstructs scalable, explorable tool-composition space from real execution traces and synthesizes long-horizon, verifiable agent tasks across diverse tool and environment combinations within this space. We show that ToolSpace plugs into long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, producing AutomationBench Pro and 𝜏3-Bench Banking Pro, which exceed their standard versions in difficulty, tool-call turns, and cross-environment breadth. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, experiments demonstrate clear advantages across model scales (8B744B). ToolSpace-744B-A40B surpasses GPT 5.6 Sol in average score (56.6 vs. 48.9) and matches Claude Opus 5. Further analyses reveal clear scaling relationships of data scale, environment scale, and task diversity with agent performance.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent Environment Scaling. Agent Environment Scaling has become an important foundation for the evolution of agent capabilities, by scaling the environments in which agents act. Simulator-style methods, exemplified by Simia (Li et al., 2025) and GenEnv (Guo et al., 2025), use an LLM as textual world model to emulate tool feedback: cheap to scale, but prone to hallucination and state inconsistency. Executable-environment methods instead synthesize databases, tools, and verifiable tasks programmatically (Dong et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), with later variants that evolve environments or whole interaction systems (He et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026) or repair them from execution feedback (Dong et al., 2026b). In all of these, the unit of scaling remains the environment (or the surrounding harness), so which tools may compose is fixed before any task is drawn. ToolSpace is complementary: it recovers tool-composition structure 3 witnessed by executions and synthesizes databases only on demand, so the same machinery can upgrade benchmarks. Graph-Based Agentic Data Synthesis. Building agent data with intrinsic dependencies on structured graphs is promising direction. For search and knowledge agents, prior work builds knowledge graphs or formalizes information seeking tasks to generate hard questions and trajectories (Tao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). For general tool use, function-signature or API-dependency graphs are walked to produce multi-turn calls and verified blueprints (Dong et al., 2026a; Prabhakar et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025); similar recipes reverse-synthesize trajectories for multimodal GUI and web agents (Zhang et al., 2025). These chains then feed SFT, agentic RL, and reflection-style training (Dong et al., 2026b; Shao et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). ToolSpace differs in where the graph comes from and what it guarantees: edges are mined by deterministic rules from adjacent real calls (Qin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) across environments, typed as data, state, or retry and weighted by witnessed frequency; walk enters training only after replay from 𝑠0 passes state, trace, and output checks. ToolSpace is the framework to make witnessed tool composition the single primitive behind cross-environment tasks and benchmarks.

An environment 𝑒 = (D, F𝑒) pairs persistent database with tool subset F𝑒 and induces state space S𝑒 with snapshots 𝑠𝑡. Data-centric environment synthesis. Prior work samples theme 𝑚, first synthesizes an underlying database 𝑝(D 𝑚), then synthesizes derived tools F𝑒 𝑝(F𝑒 D, 𝑚) conditioned jointly on the theme and the database, and further synthesizes tasks 𝑞 𝑝(𝑞 D, F𝑒). Because F𝑒 is synthetic tool set conditioned on fabricated D, its argument logic need not coincide with any real interface, and the resulting task synthesis is likewise detached from real tool-logic relations; cross-environment reachability is undefined, as tools from different (D, F𝑒) pairs share no typed relation. Tool-centric environment synthesis (our problem). Given real execution traces = {( 𝑓𝑡, 𝑥𝑡, 𝑜𝑡)}, we seek: (i) typed tool graph GTS = (V, E, 𝑤) whose tool nodes and inter-tool connections are extracted from and filtered against M; (ii) environment clusters aggregated by tool-edge density together with real tool definitions; (iii) underlying data synthesized on demand for operation environments; and (iv) dataset XTS = {(𝑞, 𝑉, 𝜔, 𝑠0)}. Each tool chain 𝜔 = (𝑣1, . . . , 𝑣𝐿) must be walk on GTS satisfying dependency reachability, state preconditions with respect to 𝑠𝑡, and parameter provenance: every argument must be traceable to 𝑞, 𝑠0, or an earlier observation 𝑜<𝑡. It must also be replay-verified, such that re-executing 𝜔 from 𝑠0 passes all assertions in 𝑉. Our objective is to maximize the longhorizon, cross-environment coverage of XTS subject to replay verification, rather than the fidelity of any single synthesized database. Under this tool-centric formulation, tools conform to real toolinterface definitions, the execution logic of synthesized tasks follows real tool-connection relations, and databases are synthesized only on demand, making synthesis efficient and cost-saving.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Overview. We present ToolSpace, tool-centric framework for cross-environment agent data synthesis (Figure 2). ToolSpace comprises two tightly coupled components, detailed below, and seamlessly raises the difficulty of existing environment benchmarks (5): Tool Space Exploration (4.1) extracts tool calls from real traces, mines data/state/retry dependencies by rules, builds tool-composition graph, clusters tools into environments, and synthesizes database only for operation-bearing clusters. Cross-Environment Task Synthesis (4.2) explores executable long-horizon chains by State-Aware Random Walks and decompiles them into tasks with verification scripts, retaining only samples that replay from 𝑠0 and pass all checks.

sections.title: 4.1.1 Agent Trajectory Collection
sections.content: To obtain diverse, large-scale real execution evidence, we build unified agent-trajectory corpus from two source families. MCP-ecosystem trajectories. Existing MCP environment scaling work (Dong et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2025) typically synthesizes task queries over real MCP servers from registries such as Smithery. Because their tool definitions come from real servers, such tasks can be seamlessly re-executed against the live services. We collect real tool catalog from the registry, keep only tasks whose tool definitions exactly match the real servers, execute them with diverse agents on real MCP services, and record the complete call chains as MMCP. Web-sourced agent trajectories. We additionally use deep-search agent to collect general tool-use trajectories from the web. We group them by execution provenance, rank them from high to low by the degree of execution authenticity, and apply progressively stricter filtering to lower-authenticity data: Real-server interaction trajectories (High). We retain records executed on real services. Toucan1.5M (Xu et al., 2025) covers 495 MCP servers, 2,000+ tools, and 1.5M trajectories, with synthetic instructions but real executions. ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) covers 16,464 RapidAPI interfaces and 469K API calls; we remove unavailable interfaces. Real-workspace interaction trajectories (Medium). We collect trajectories executed by SWEagent (Yang et al., 2024) and OpenHands (Wang et al., 2025) in real containers and repositories. We retain only explicit tool calls and exclude shell wrappers such as execute_bash. Synthetic-tool trajectories (Low). We collect trajectories generated in synthetic environments (Dong et al., 2026a,b; Song et al., 2026). Because of potential tool inconsistency, we retain only calls whose tool names and schema formats match corresponding real tools. The three groups merge into Mopen; all tool calls form = MMCP Mopen = {( 𝑓𝑡, 𝑥𝑡, 𝑜𝑡)}, (2) where ( 𝑓𝑡, 𝑥𝑡, 𝑜𝑡) is the 𝑡-th call of trajectory: 𝑓𝑡 the tool, 𝑥𝑡 its inputs, and 𝑜𝑡 its result. Calls within trajectory keep their order. 4.1.2 Tool-Space Graph Modeling To explicitly model these implicit tool relations, we organize into typed tool-composition graph GTS = (V, E, 𝑤) that can chain different services into one tool world (Figure 2). 5 Figure 2: Overview of the ToolSpace framework. Concrete State dependency (𝑣𝑡 state 𝑣𝑡+1): the first call mutates an environment object and the second call reads or further mutates the same object, not merely coincidentally equal value. Consequently, GTS captures tool transitions during execution rather than merely listing available tools.

We cluster the weighted undirected projection of GTS by connection density and organize the clusters using the environment and tool configurations of real MCP services. This produces = {𝑐1, . . . , 𝑐𝐾 } with 𝐾 = 804, where each cluster defines an environment 𝑒𝑘 = (D𝑘, F𝑘) with tool set F𝑘 and database D𝑘. We consider three cases: Operation environments. These environments contain tools that create, modify, or delete objects and therefore require an underlying database. Following Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026a), we derive theme 𝑚𝑘 from each cluster and use research agent Gres, built on policy model 𝜋𝜃 and tools Tres, to collect and align web data: (0) 𝑘 = Gres(𝑚𝑘; 𝜋𝜃, Tres). Many state-query tools return partial snapshots of the environment, such as google_drive.files.list and gmail.users.messages.get. We use these outputs as anchors to initialize the relevant environment state rather than synthesizing database from scratch. The resulting state serves as the initial snapshot 𝑠0. sections.content: To more comprehensively showcase ToolSpace, Figures 4 and 5 characterize the static statistics of ToolSpaces graph, environments, and synthesized tasks. (A) Graph Scale and Dependency Structure. Reconstructed from collected tool-call trajectories, GTS contains 77,760 tool-call-pattern nodes derived from 2,042 distinct canonical tools. Its mean and maximum outdegrees (outgoing dependency edges per node) are 2.3 and 56, respectively. Panel (a) presents word cloud of the environment types covered by ToolSpace synthesis, including Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, Google Drive, Salesforce, and Airtable. Panel (d) shows that data, state, and retry edges account for 69%, 25%, and 6%, respectively. The dominance of data edges indicates that tool composition is driven primarily by intermediate-result transfer, while state and retry edges capture state prerequisites and failure recovery. Every edge is witnessed by adjacent calls in real trajectories, providing execution-grounded tool reachability. 9 (B) Environment Diversity and Selective Grounding. The reference inventory covers 804 real MCP environments. Figure 4(b) identifies Communication & General Utilities, Finance & Markets, and Document & Design as the largest domains, accounting for 27.4%, 11.2%, and 10.1% of environments, respectively. Table 1 reports performance on seven benchmarks. ToolSpace is strong across model scales; three observations summarize this. (1) Environment scaling learns the form of function calling, not tool orchestration. All 78B environment scaling baselines remain weak (<10) on the cross-environment, long-horizon suites AutomationBench, 𝜏3-Bench Banking, JobBench, and Harvey LAB. Single-environment data therefore correct the form of calls without teaching cross-environment composition. (2) ToolSpace exhibits cross-environment long-horizon execution across scales. Gains hold in each domain: ToolSpace-8B leads same-size environment scaling baselines on real productivity suites such as AutomationBench, JobBench, and OfficeQA Pro; ToolSpace-35B-A3B exceeds its Qwen backbone on all seven benchmarks, with AutomationBench rising by more than 35 points (8.245.8). The pattern persists to 744B: ToolSpace-744B-A40B surpasses GLM 5.3, GPT 5.6 Sol, and its teacher policy K3 on average, and matches Claude Opus 5. These consistent gains across model scales, including performance beyond the teacher, argue against simple capability distillation and instead indicate that ToolSpace teaches transferable tool-composition structure for cross-environment execution. (3) On-policy agent RL further unlocks capacity. SFT alone lifts ToolSpace by 18.0 points over the 35B backbone (23.041.0). On-policy RL on ToolSpace data adds further 2.2 points at 35B (41.043.2), with the largest gain on 𝜏3-Bench Banking (34.042.3), showing that environment RL still leaves room for improvement. This indicates that on-policy environment RL can, through exploration, further unlock the multi-tool orchestration potential of SFT-trained models.

sections.content: To test whether ToolSpace raises frontier-benchmark difficulty, Table 2 compares seven frontier models on the two Pro splits with Standard. All seven frontier models drop substantially from Standard to Pro. Even Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.1 Sol fall by 32.9 and 26.1 points on AutomationBench, and by 15.8 and 16.8 points on 𝜏3-Bench Banking, respectively; the largest AutomationBench drop reaches 38.2 points. sections.content: Environment Scaling Analysis. To examine whether the breadth of the tool space matters independently of data volume, we fine-tune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on data synthesized from increasing fractions of ToolSpace environments, from 1/16 to the full environment set. The backbone, training configuration, and evaluation protocol are held fixed, and zero denotes the untuned backbone. Figure 7(b) 13 Figure 7: Data and environment scaling results. (a) Data scaling by training-data fraction. (b) Environment scaling by training-environment fraction. Zero denotes the untuned Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone. Figure 8: Task-Synthesis Diversity Visualization. Synthesized task embeddings colored by DBSCAN cluster. reports the results. Despite fluctuations at intermediate fractions, performance improves overall with environment scale and reaches the full-setting optimum, following clear scaling trend. The increase on AutomationBench between 1/16 and 1/8 is particularly sharp, from 9.2 to 33.8. This suggests that new environment clusters contribute new cross-environment edges, and that space breadth is the limiting factor when coverage is low. In contrast, 𝜏3-Bench Banking improves more slowly under environment scaling, which is consistent with its reliance on narrower set of stateful banking tools. This supports the central motivation of ToolSpace: performance scales with the breadth of environments that witnessed chains connect. From the perspective of sustained scaling returns, AutomationBench gains about +4 points per doubling beyond 1/8 on average, despite plateau between 1/4 and 1/2, while 𝜏3-Bench Banking shows its largest jump only at the full environment set (19.634.0), indicating that highly connected environment clusters contribute late. Data Scaling Analysis. To examine whether the benefit of ToolSpace grows with the amount of synthesized data, we fine-tune Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on increasing fractions of the ToolSpace SFT dataset, namely 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, and the full dataset. The backbone, training configuration, and evaluation protocol are held fixed, and zero denotes the untuned backbone. Figure 7(a) reports the results. Performance improves overall as more data are used, and the full dataset performs best on all five benchmarks. SkillsBench shows small intermediate decrease from 32.4 at 1/16 to 32.0 at 1/8. AutomationBench rises from 25.2 at 1/16 to 45.8 with the full dataset, and 𝜏3-Bench Banking rises from 20.6 to 34.0. The gain is therefore not explained by small set of high-quality examples. Each additional fraction contributes new witnessed tool chains and dependency structures, which is consistent with our motivation that capability grows from the composition space covered by the data. The small decreases below the backbone at the 1/16 fraction on BFCL V4 and OfficeQA Pro indicate 14 Figure 9: Environment relevance and synthesis cost. (a) Effect of environment relevance: Full, Top 50%, and Random 50% environments; Δ is the TopRandom gap. (b) Environment synthesis cost proxy: synthesized files by type over 500 sampled environments. interference when the SFT mixture is too small, and the trend becomes stable once the data fraction increases. This demonstrates the scalability of ToolSpaces synthesized data. From the perspective of sustained scaling returns, the step from 1/2 to the full dataset still improves all five benchmarks (AutomationBench +4.6), with no plateau, indicating that the current synthesis scale has not yet hit the returns ceiling of data volume. Environment Relevance Analysis. To verify that ToolSpaces gains do not stem from overfitting to benchmark-like environments, we rank environment clusters by relevance to each benchmark using BGE (Chen et al., 2024) embeddings, and compare SFT on (i) the full data, (ii) only the top-50% most relevant environments (Top-50%), and (iii) random 50% of environments (Random50%) (Figure 9(a)). If the gains were driven by benchmark-specific environment fitting, Top-50% should substantially outperform Random-50%. Random-50% uses the same number of environments but excludes many of the most relevant ones. Instead, the two differ by at most 1.7 points on AutomationBench, SkillsBench, BFCL V4, and OfficeQA Pro, and both approach full-data performance using only half the environments. ToolSpaces gains therefore do not hinge on benchmark-aligned environments, but reflect transferable tool-composition structure. Task-Synthesis Diversity Visualization. We examine whether ToolSpace spans broader space of environments and tasks than prior environment-scaling methods by randomly sampling 2k questions from four SFT corpora (EnvScaler, Agent-World, Agent-Reflex, and ToolSpace). We employ BGEM3 (Chen et al., 2024) as the embedding model, apply t-SNE for dimensionality reduction, and use DBSCAN (Ester et al., 1996) for clustering. As shown in Figure 8, ToolSpace forms the largest number of question clusters (42), compared with EnvScaler, Agent-World, and Agent-Reflex (25, 31, and 34, respectively), while retaining compact local groupings and broader coverage of the embedding space. This pattern suggests that ToolSpace expands task-space coverage beyond prior environment-scaling methods. We attribute the gain to edge-weighted sampling over observed tool compositions, which connects wider range of environments. Environment Synthesis Cost Analysis. We estimate ToolSpaces environment synthesis cost savings using the number of synthesized files as proxy. From 500 environments randomly sampled from Agent-Worlds public library, we identify the files that ToolSpace would need to synthesize. Because file generation and validation complexity may vary, this proxy does not directly measure token, wall-clock, API, or compute cost. As shown in Figure 9(b), Agent-World synthesizes all 2,724 files in the sample, whereas ToolSpace synthesizes only 1,218 files associated with operation-bearing environments1,506 fewer files, or 55.3% reduction. This reduction follows from ToolSpaces selective-grounding strategy: persistent artifacts are materialized only for operation-bearing environments, while recorded returns are reused for stateless interactions. Beyond which environments are selected and how much they cost to synthesize, we finally examine which ToolSpace components drive the gains. Table 3 reports component ablation of ToolSpace at 35B, where w/o denotes removing or replacing one specific component. We make three observations. (1) Removing any component degrades all five benchmarks, showing that the components are complementary rather than redundant. (2) The two structural edge types divide the labor: state edges matter most for 𝜏3-Bench Banking and AutomationBench, where state preconditions decide whether chain is executable at all, while data edges matter most for BFCL V4 and OfficeQA Pro, where argument provenance carries the task. Their comparable average drops (7.1 vs. 7.4 points) fall on disjoint benchmarks, confirming that state dependencies, not data flow alone, enable crossenvironment execution. (3) How edges are obtained and traversed matters as much as which edges exist: LLM-judged edges degrade every benchmark almost as much as removing state edges, so edges must be witnessed by execution rather than merely plausible; rollback and edge-weighted sampling contribute in between, and retry edges have the smallest effect, consistent with their role in robustness to noisy tools.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we present ToolSpace, tool-centric framework for cross-environment agent data synthesis. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies between adjacent calls in execution traces from real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and 𝜏3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.
